newsitem.title: UK: HEAVY RAIN MEANS FRUSTRATION FOR EUROPE GRAINS MKT.
newsitem.headline: HEAVY RAIN MEANS FRUSTRATION FOR EUROPE GRAINS MKT.

text.p: Heavy rain delaying harvesting in many areas set a frustrating tone for the European grains market.
Traders complained that supply was coming too slow and worried about the effects on quality of downpours which produced floods in some areas.
Foul weather lifted prices in France as sellers disappeared and premiums soared as high as 100 francs a tonne for best wheat with guarantees, over the price of standard quality wheat.
Harvesting has reached the grain areas north of Paris which had some of the strongest downpours between Tuesday and Thursday, though the northeastern tip of France was spared.
The tussle with the European Commission over export licences had less effect though a decision to grant 470,000 tonnes of soft wheat for export lent some support, traders said.
French wheat is uncompetitive however at the current six Ecus per tonne tax as Iraq and Morocco, and possibly soon Egypt, scout for wheat.
Friday's finer weather also took a bit of steam out of the market ahead of the weekend, traders said.
Traders said there was talk of falling test weight results, affecting quality, and early germination caused by wet weather. But it was impossible to gauge the extent of the damage so far.
Maize was supported by sporadic buying which had mostly fizzled out by Friday. Barley markets were quiet.
German grain sellers were maintaining high nominal export prices for wheat although there was no fresh buying.
Fob Baltic offers of 13 percent protein wheat are at 287.50 marks a tonne, basis 3,000 tonnes.

Internal prices were undergoing large swings depending on the progress of the domestic harvest, which has just about started for wheat in the south and west, as well as news input from progress in other European countries.
Impact from nearing harvest pressure was mostly offset by farmer and merchant demand but demand from end consumers in the milling industry was non-existent.

Bread rye prices benefitted from recent EU export allocations for German intervention rye but feed rye prices were easing amid harvest pressure from competing barley and triticale, a wheat/rye hybrid.
This also weighed on feed wheat prices.
Ex-farm prices of barley at wholesale level are at 200-220 marks.
In the UK a stop-start harvest has made life frustrating for traders, especially as farmers were loth to sell at current low prices.
The harvest was more stop than start in southern areas, with heavy rain hitting the south-west in particular.

Sterling's fall on Thursday, which carried through to Friday helped underpin the market. The rise in grains prices went too far for the fall in sterling, one trader said. "Sterling's down 1.5 percent and grains are up three percent," one said.
Exporting has not been a big issue for the trade. "This market isn't export led," one trader said. "There are no sales of UK grain to continental consumers going on at all," another said.
Trading slowed down to a trickle in Spain, dulled by the traditional August exodus to the beach.
Relentless damp weather this year has meant that crop quality variation is high, market participants said.
"With all the rain we've had, its almost impossible to talk about a clear prices trend," said one trader in the north.
Durum wheat was scarcely offered, he added.
He estimated that about 70 percent of the total barley crop has been collected. "Barley quality is pretty good, although there's also been some very average harvests," he added.

Milling wheat quality is poor in Spain this year, as in the rest of Europe, and for that reason the spread of prices was wide. "The decent stuff has been offered at a about 29,000 pesetas, but there's also poor crop available at 24,000 pesetas," said one trader.
Maize meanwhile is developing well, with both quality and quantity expected to be healthy this year. Maize will start to be harvested in the north in about September.
Italian grain markets were largely closed and were likely to be mainly untraded through most of August because of the holiday period.
